title: Editing & Proofreading
subtitle: Master proofreading conventions, correct the classic French error types, and rewrite a text for a new audience

lessons.title: La relecture
lessons.description: The proofreader's craft: correction marks, the logic of a careful reread, and the French typographic conventions — spacing before punctuation, capitalisation, quotation marks — that a professional relecture enforces.

blocks.heading: La relecture : un métier, pas un coup d'œil
blocks.body: Proofreading a finished text is not the same skill as writing it — the writer's eye keeps sliding over what it expects to see, while a proofreader trains themselves to see what is actually printed. Professional relecture usually happens in at least two passes: one for meaning and structure, a second, slower pass devoted entirely to spelling, agreement, and typography, often read aloud or even backwards to break the reader's habit of anticipating the next word.

examples.french: L'œil de l'auteur voit ce qu'il a voulu écrire, pas toujours ce qui est réellement sur la page.
examples.english: The author's eye sees what they meant to write, not always what is actually on the page.

examples.french: Une bonne relecture se fait en au moins deux passes : le sens d'abord, la forme ensuite.
examples.english: A good proofread happens in at least two passes: meaning first, then form.

examples.french: Lire un texte à voix haute ralentit l'œil et révèle des fautes qu'une lecture silencieuse laisse filer.
examples.english: Reading a text aloud slows the eye down and reveals mistakes a silent reading lets slip by.

examples.french: Certains correcteurs relisent une dernière fois à l'envers, phrase par phrase, pour ne plus se laisser porter par le sens.
examples.english: Some proofreaders do one last pass backwards, sentence by sentence, so they can no longer be carried along by the meaning.

examples.french: La relecture n'invente rien : elle vérifie que le texte dit exactement ce que l'auteur croit avoir écrit.
examples.english: Proofreading invents nothing: it checks that the text says exactly what the author believes they wrote.

blocks.tip: When proofreading your own French writing, read it aloud slowly — your ear catches missing agreements and awkward spacing that your eye has already learned to skip over.

blocks.heading: Les signes de correction : un langage à part
blocks.body: French copy-editors share a small, standardised vocabulary of correction marks — a wavy underline for a doubtful word, a caret for an insertion, a looping delete mark, 'stet' written in the margin to cancel a previous correction — that lets several people annotate the same proof without confusion. Knowing this shorthand matters at C2 not because you will necessarily mark up paper proofs, but because editors still describe corrections in speech using this vocabulary: 'il y a une coquille à corriger', 'ce passage est à revoir'.

examples.french: Le signe de correction en marge indique précisément où et comment intervenir.
examples.english: The correction mark in the margin indicates precisely where and how to intervene.

examples.french: Une coquille s'était glissée dans le titre, et personne ne l'avait vue avant l'impression.
examples.english: A typo had slipped into the headline, and no one had spotted it before printing.

examples.french: Le correcteur signale la faute sans jamais réécrire la phrase à la place de l'auteur.
examples.english: The proofreader flags the mistake without ever rewriting the sentence in the author's place.

examples.french: Sur l'épreuve, chaque intervention est datée et signée, pour qu'on sache qui a corrigé quoi.
examples.english: On the proof, every intervention is dated and signed, so everyone knows who corrected what.

examples.french: Un comité de lecture propose des corrections ; l'auteur garde toujours le dernier mot.
examples.english: An editorial board proposes corrections; the author always has the final say.

blocks.tip: In professional French publishing, 'stet' (from Latin, 'let it stand') is still used in the margin to cancel a mark someone else made — worth recognising even if you never use it yourself.

blocks.heading: La typographie française : des règles très précises
blocks.body: French typography enforces rules that look pedantic to English speakers but are non-negotiable in careful French prose: a space (traditionally a thin, non-breaking one) before « ; », « : », « ? », « ! », and inside French quotation marks « comme ceci » — but no space before a comma or a full stop. Getting this wrong is the single fastest way for a proofread French text to look unproofread, even when every word is correctly spelled.

examples.french: Ça va ? demande-t-elle, sans jamais coller le point d'interrogation au dernier mot.
examples.english: "Is everything all right?" she asks, never letting the question mark run into the last word.

examples.french: Il a répondu : « Non merci, pas aujourd'hui. »
examples.english: He replied: "No thank you, not today."

examples.french: Les guillemets français s'ouvrent et se referment avec un espace insécable, contrairement aux guillemets anglais.
examples.english: French quotation marks open and close with a non-breaking space, unlike English quotation marks.

examples.french: On écrit « vingt-cinq », avec un trait d'union, mais « cent trente », sans trait d'union avant « trente ».
examples.english: You write "twenty-five" with a hyphen, but "one hundred thirty" without a hyphen before "thirty".

examples.french: Une virgule ne prend jamais d'espace avant elle, seulement après.
examples.english: A comma never takes a space before it, only after.

blocks.tip: Memorise the rule as a single sentence: double punctuation marks (: ; ? !) and French quotes want a space before them in French; simple ones (, .) never do.

blocks.heading: L'espacement devant la ponctuation double
blocks.body: French, unlike English, inserts a space before every 'double' punctuation mark — the colon, semicolon, question mark, exclamation mark — and before and after French quotation marks « », because these marks were historically set as separate pieces of type needing visual room. Simple punctuation (comma, full stop, ellipsis) never takes a space before it. A proofreader who lets this slip is committing the most visible typographic fault in French editing, even in an otherwise flawless text.

blocks.heading: La majuscule après les deux-points et dans les titres
blocks.body: French keeps a lower-case letter after a colon unless what follows is a full, independent quoted sentence or begins a genuinely new statement — the opposite of the English habit of routinely capitalising after a colon. In titles, French capitalises only the first word (and any proper nouns within it), never every significant word the way English headline style does; 'Le Rouge et le Noir' keeps its capital on 'Noir' only because it is itself a proper adjective-turned-title element, an exception rather than the rule.

passages.title: Le métier de l'ombre
passages.french: On ne remarque un correcteur que lorsqu'il a manqué quelque chose. C'est là toute l'ironie d'un métier qui consiste à disparaître derrière le texte : une relecture réussie ne laisse aucune trace, sinon l'absence gênante de toute faute. Le correcteur ne réécrit pas, ne réorganise pas, ne juge pas le fond ; il vérifie que la forme sert fidèlement ce que l'auteur a voulu dire, jusque dans le moindre espace avant un point d'interrogation. Certains maisons d'édition emploient encore des relecteurs qui travaillent en binôme, chacun lisant le texte de l'autre à voix haute pendant que le second suit des yeux sur l'épreuve : la voix ralentit ce que l'œil, seul, aurait laissé filer. D'autres préfèrent la relecture à l'envers, phrase par phrase depuis la fin, méthode contre-intuitive mais redoutablement efficace contre les fautes d'accord, puisqu'elle empêche le cerveau de deviner la suite avant de l'avoir lue. Le correcteur automatique, aussi perfectionné soit-il, ne remplace aucune de ces deux méthodes : il confond encore, avec une belle constance, « leur » et « leurs », ou ne voit rien d'anormal dans une phrase grammaticalement correcte mais absurde. La relecture reste, en somme, un travail d'humain patient, au service d'un texte qui, bien fait, ne devrait jamais laisser deviner qu'on y a touché.
passages.english: You only notice a proofreader when they have missed something. That is the whole irony of a profession that consists of disappearing behind the text: a successful proofread leaves no trace, other than the awkward absence of any mistake. The proofreader does not rewrite, does not reorganise, does not judge the substance; they check that the form faithfully serves what the author meant to say, down to the smallest space before a question mark. Some publishing houses still employ proofreaders who work in pairs, one reading the text aloud while the other follows along on the proof: the voice slows down what the eye alone would have let slip by. Others prefer backwards proofreading, sentence by sentence from the end, a counter-intuitive but formidably effective method against agreement errors, since it stops the brain from guessing what comes next before actually reading it. The spell-checker, however sophisticated, replaces neither of these methods: it still confuses, with impressive consistency, "leur" and "leurs", or sees nothing wrong with a sentence that is grammatically correct but absurd. Proofreading remains, in the end, a work of patient humans, in the service of a text that, done well, should never let anyone guess it was ever touched.

lessons.title: Corriger un texte
lessons.description: The classic French error types even fluent native speakers make: past-participle agreement edge cases, treacherous homophones like ça/sa and ces/ses, and the syntax mistakes a careful editor learns to catch on sight.

blocks.heading: Les fautes que même les Français font
blocks.body: A short list of error types accounts for most mistakes in careful adult French writing — not beginner mistakes, but traps built into the language itself: agreement rules with exceptions inside exceptions, and a startling number of words that sound identical but are spelled, and function, completely differently. A good corrector does not simply 'know French better'; they have memorised exactly which constructions to double-check every single time, because native fluency alone does not protect against these traps.

examples.french: Même un rédacteur expérimenté relit deux fois toute phrase contenant un participe passé complexe.
examples.english: Even an experienced writer rereads twice any sentence containing a tricky past participle.

examples.french: Ces fautes ne trahissent pas un manque de culture, mais des pièges intégrés à la langue elle-même.
examples.english: These mistakes do not betray a lack of education, but traps built into the language itself.

examples.french: Un correcteur professionnel connaît par cœur la liste des confusions les plus fréquentes.
examples.english: A professional proofreader knows the list of the most frequent confusions by heart.

examples.french: L'oral pardonne ce que l'écrit, lui, ne pardonne jamais.
examples.english: Speech forgives what writing never does.

examples.french: Se relire avec méfiance, c'est déjà la moitié du travail de correction.
examples.english: Rereading your own work with suspicion is already half the job of correcting it.

blocks.tip: Treat every sentence with a past participle, or a homophone pair, as an automatic checkpoint — even when the sentence sounds perfectly natural out loud.

blocks.heading: Les homophones qui piègent tout le monde
blocks.body: French is unusually rich in homophones that sort into entirely different grammatical categories — 'ça' (pronoun) versus 'sa' (possessive adjective), 'c'est' (it is) versus 's'est' (reflexive past), 'ces' (these) versus 'ses' (his/her, plural) — and because they sound identical, the only reliable test is grammatical, not phonetic: what part of speech does the sentence actually need here? Learning the quick substitution tests native speakers use internally, often without realising it, is the fastest way to stop guessing.

examples.french: Ça ne se discute pas ; sa décision est prise.
examples.english: That's not up for discussion; her decision is made.

examples.french: C'est décidé : elle s'est enfin lancée.
examples.english: It's decided: she has finally taken the plunge.

examples.french: Ces documents appartiennent à ses collègues, pas à lui.
examples.english: These documents belong to her colleagues, not to him.

examples.french: Pour distinguer « ces » et « ses », remplacez par « ceux-là » ou par « les siens » : le sens tranche aussitôt.
examples.english: To tell "ces" from "ses" apart, try substituting "those ones" or "his/hers": the meaning settles it at once.

examples.french: Remplacer « s'est » par « s'était » à l'imparfait confirme qu'il s'agit bien d'un verbe pronominal.
examples.english: Substituting "s'était" in the imperfect confirms it really is a reflexive verb.

blocks.tip: When in doubt between a homophone pair, mentally swap in a word from the same category that cannot be confused ('cela' for 'ça', 'la sienne' for 'sa') — if the sentence still makes sense, you have the right word.

blocks.heading: L'accord du participe passé : les cas qui résistent
blocks.body: The core rule is simple — with 'avoir', the past participle agrees with a preceding direct object, not with the subject — but several constructions resist it: pronominal verbs where the reflexive pronoun is an indirect object ('elles se sont parlé', no agreement, because 'parler à quelqu'un' takes an indirect object), a participle followed by an infinitive that agrees only if the preceding object is doing the action of that infinitive, and the deliberately invariable 'fait' and 'laissé' before an infinitive. These exceptions are exactly what separates a merely fluent writer from a genuinely careful one.

blocks.heading: Les verbes pronominaux : le piège de l'objet indirect
blocks.body: Reflexive verbs agree with the reflexive pronoun exactly as any past participle agrees with a preceding direct object — which means that when the underlying verb takes an indirect object ('parler à quelqu'un', 'téléphoner à quelqu'un', 'se plaire à quelque chose'), the reflexive pronoun is indirect too, and the participle stays invariable. The only reliable test is to ask what the non-pronominal verb takes: 'parler à' takes 'à', so 'ils se sont parlé' never agrees, while 'regarder quelqu'un' takes a direct object, so 'ils se sont regardés' does.

blocks.tip: Before agreeing a pronominal participle, mentally strip out 'se' and ask what the plain verb takes: 'à quelqu'un' means no agreement, a direct object means agreement follows the usual rule.

blocks.heading: Le participe passé suivi d'un infinitif
blocks.body: When a past participle like 'entendu', 'vu', 'senti', or 'laissé' is followed by an infinitive, it agrees with the preceding direct object only if that object is actually performing the action of the infinitive — not merely undergoing it. 'Les chanteurs que j'ai entendus chanter' agrees, because the singers are the ones singing; 'la chanson que j'ai entendu chanter' does not, because the song is not doing the singing, it is being sung. 'Fait' is the sole absolute exception: it never agrees before an infinitive, full stop.

passages.title: Le courrier des lecteurs pointilleux
passages.french: Chaque semaine, le service courrier du journal reçoit une poignée de lettres qui ne portent que sur des fautes. Non sur le fond des articles, non sur les opinions défendues, mais sur une virgule mal placée, un « ça » écrit pour « sa », un participe passé resté au masculin quand il aurait dû s'accorder. Le rédacteur en chef appelle ces lecteurs, avec une tendresse un peu résignée, les « chasseurs de coquilles ». Ils ont, en général, parfaitement raison, et c'est bien ce qui rend leur vigilance à la fois précieuse et un peu épuisante. Un correcteur du journal confie qu'il redoute davantage un homophone mal choisi qu'une erreur factuelle, parce que le lecteur pardonne plus facilement une date fausse, vite corrigée dans l'édition suivante, qu'une faute d'accord, qui semble trahir un manque de rigueur plus profond. La rédaction a fini par établir une liste, mise à jour chaque année, des pièges les plus signalés par le courrier : « ces » et « ses » arrivent en tête, suivis de près par « quoique » écrit en deux mots là où il n'en faut qu'un, et par l'éternel accord du participe passé avec « avoir ». On pourrait croire cette vigilance excessive, presque maniaque, jusqu'à ce qu'on se souvienne qu'une seule coquille, republiée sans correction, se retrouve citée, copiée, reproduite ailleurs, avec la même autorité involontaire qu'un fait vérifié. La relecture, en somme, ne protège pas seulement le journal ; elle protège tous ceux qui, plus tard, croiront pouvoir s'y fier sans vérifier davantage.
passages.english: Every week, the newspaper's mail service receives a handful of letters concerned only with mistakes. Not with the substance of the articles, not with the opinions defended, but with a misplaced comma, a "ça" written where "sa" belonged, a past participle left masculine when it should have agreed. The editor-in-chief calls these readers, with a somewhat resigned fondness, the "typo hunters". They are, generally, entirely right, and that is exactly what makes their vigilance both precious and a little exhausting. One of the paper's proofreaders admits dreading a wrongly chosen homophone more than a factual error, because readers forgive a wrong date, quickly corrected in the next edition, more easily than an agreement mistake, which seems to betray a deeper lack of rigour. The editorial team eventually drew up a list, updated every year, of the traps most often flagged by readers' mail: "ces" and "ses" come out on top, closely followed by "quoique" written as two words where it should be one, and the ever-present agreement of the past participle with "avoir". One might think this vigilance excessive, almost obsessive, until remembering that a single typo, republished without correction, ends up quoted, copied, reproduced elsewhere, with the same unintended authority as a verified fact. Proofreading, in the end, does not only protect the newspaper; it protects everyone who will later believe they can rely on it without checking any further.

lessons.title: Réécrire pour un public
lessons.description: Rewriting the same content for a different audience: how register, sentence length, vocabulary, and even punctuation shift when a text moves from expert readers to the general public, or from a formal report to a casual briefing.

blocks.heading: Le même contenu, un autre public
blocks.body: Rewriting for a new audience is not translation and not summary — the facts stay identical, but the vocabulary, sentence length, and the amount of background explanation all shift to meet what the target reader already knows and needs. A good editor starts by asking one question before touching a single word: what does this reader already know, and what would lose them if I assumed it? Everything else — register, tone, structure — follows from that single answer.

examples.french: Réécrire pour un public, ce n'est pas simplifier le fond, c'est ajuster la forme.
examples.english: Rewriting for an audience is not simplifying the substance, it is adjusting the form.

examples.french: La première question à se poser est toujours la même : que sait déjà ce lecteur-là ?
examples.english: The first question to ask is always the same: what does this particular reader already know?

examples.french: Un même fait scientifique se raconte différemment à un confrère et à un enfant de dix ans.
examples.english: The same scientific fact is told differently to a colleague and to a ten-year-old.

examples.french: Changer de destinataire, c'est changer de longueur de phrase avant même de changer de mots.
examples.english: Changing the intended reader means changing sentence length before even changing the words.

examples.french: Le contenu ne ment jamais ; c'est la forme qui décide si le lecteur reste ou abandonne.
examples.english: The content never lies; it is the form that decides whether the reader stays or gives up.

blocks.tip: Before rewriting a single sentence, write one line describing the target reader's existing knowledge — everything you draft afterwards should answer to that description.

blocks.heading: Le registre : soutenu, courant, familier
blocks.body: French recognises three broad registers — soutenu (formal, literary), courant (neutral, everyday), and familier (colloquial) — and a rewrite almost always moves a text between them: a legal report rewritten for a general newspaper drops from soutenu towards courant, while an internal memo turned into a casual briefing might drop as far as familier. The danger is not choosing the wrong register outright, but mixing registers within the same paragraph, which reads as an error even when every individual sentence is grammatically correct.

examples.french: Le registre soutenu privilégie le vocabulaire précis et les phrases longues et structurées.
examples.english: The formal register favours precise vocabulary and long, structured sentences.

examples.french: Le registre courant reste correct sans jamais chercher l'effet ni l'ornement.
examples.english: The neutral register stays correct without ever seeking effect or ornament.

examples.french: Le registre familier tolère l'ellipse, l'apostrophe directe au lecteur, et un vocabulaire plus concret.
examples.english: The colloquial register tolerates ellipsis, direct address to the reader, and more concrete vocabulary.

examples.french: Mélanger les registres dans un même paragraphe sonne faux, même sans la moindre faute de grammaire.
examples.english: Mixing registers within the same paragraph rings false, even without a single grammatical mistake.

examples.french: Le niveau de langue se choisit une fois pour tout le texte, pas phrase par phrase.
examples.english: The level of language is chosen once for the whole text, not sentence by sentence.

blocks.tip: If you catch yourself switching between 'vous' and casual asides within one paragraph, that is usually the first symptom of a register mix that needs fixing.

blocks.heading: Les gestes concrets de la réécriture
blocks.body: A handful of concrete moves cover most register shifts: 'alléger' cuts subordinate clauses into shorter, independent sentences; 'étoffer' adds the background context an expert text takes for granted; 'reformuler' replaces technical vocabulary with everyday equivalents while flagging what nuance is lost; and 'condenser' does the reverse, tightening an over-explained popular text back into the compact density a specialist reader expects. Knowing which move a given rewrite needs — often several at once — is the practical core of the whole exercise.

examples.french: Allégez une phrase de trente mots en la coupant en deux, sans en perdre l'idée.
examples.english: Lighten a thirty-word sentence by splitting it in two, without losing the idea.

examples.french: Étoffez ce qu'un expert tiendrait pour acquis, mais qu'un profane ignore complètement.
examples.english: Flesh out what an expert would take for granted but a layperson has no idea of.

examples.french: Reformuler un jargon technique, c'est traduire sans trahir, en signalant ce que l'on simplifie.
examples.english: Rephrasing technical jargon means translating without betraying, while flagging what is being simplified.

examples.french: Condensez un texte de vulgarisation pour un lectorat déjà expert : il n'a pas besoin des explications de base.
examples.english: Condense a popular-science text for an already expert readership: they don't need the basic explanations.

examples.french: Vulgariser sans mentir demande souvent plus de travail que d'écrire pour des spécialistes.
examples.english: Popularising without lying often takes more work than writing for specialists.

blocks.tip: Treat 'alléger', 'étoffer', 'reformuler', and 'condenser' as four separate tools, not synonyms — the right rewrite usually needs exactly one of them for a given passage, never all four at once.

blocks.heading: Nominalisation contre verbes : monter ou descendre en registre
blocks.body: Formal French leans heavily on nominalisation — turning a verb into an abstract noun ('décider' becomes 'la prise de décision', 'analyser' becomes 'l'analyse') — because abstract nouns sound weightier and more official. Rewriting downward towards a general audience usually means reversing this: putting the action back into a plain conjugated verb with a clear human subject. Rewriting upward does the opposite, trading a lively verb for its nominalised cousin.

examples.french: La mise en œuvre du dispositif a été confiée à un comité restreint. → Un petit comité s'est chargé d'appliquer le dispositif.
examples.english: The implementation of the scheme was entrusted to a small committee. → A small committee took charge of applying the scheme.

examples.french: La révision du texte a permis une clarification substantielle. → En révisant le texte, on l'a rendu bien plus clair.
examples.english: The revision of the text allowed for substantial clarification. → By revising the text, it was made much clearer.

examples.french: L'analyse des résultats a révélé une tendance inattendue. → En analysant les résultats, on a découvert une tendance inattendue.
examples.english: The analysis of the results revealed an unexpected trend. → When analysing the results, an unexpected trend was discovered.

examples.french: Sa décision de partir a surpris tout le monde. → Il a décidé de partir, et cela a surpris tout le monde.
examples.english: His decision to leave surprised everyone. → He decided to leave, and that surprised everyone.

examples.french: Pour un public non spécialiste, préférez toujours le verbe conjugué au nom abstrait qu'il cache.
examples.english: For a non-specialist audience, always prefer the conjugated verb to the abstract noun hiding it.

blocks.tip: Scan a formal draft for nouns ending in -tion, -ment, -age; each one is a verb in disguise, and unmasking it is usually the fastest way to make a sentence sound less bureaucratic.

blocks.heading: Le conditionnel et le subjonctif pour adoucir le ton
blocks.body: Downward rewrites for a wary or non-expert reader often reach for the conditional to soften an assertion ('cela pourrait expliquer' rather than 'cela explique') and for constructions that hedge certainty without sounding evasive — a register move rather than a grammatical error. Upward rewrites for an expert or contractual audience do the reverse, replacing hedged conditionals with flat indicatives that state a claim as settled fact.

examples.french: Cela pourrait expliquer la baisse observée, sans qu'on en soit encore certain.
examples.english: This could explain the observed decline, though it isn't yet certain.

examples.french: Il semblerait que le phénomène touche surtout les zones urbaines.
examples.english: The phenomenon seems to affect mainly urban areas.

examples.french: On aurait tort de conclure trop vite à partir d'un seul cas.
examples.english: It would be a mistake to draw hasty conclusions from a single case.

examples.french: Pour un rapport contractuel, on remplacera « pourrait expliquer » par « explique », sans détour.
examples.english: For a contractual report, "could explain" is replaced by a flat "explains", with no hedging.

examples.french: Adoucir n'est pas mentir : c'est signaler honnêtement le degré de certitude du propos.
examples.english: Softening is not lying: it is honestly signalling the degree of certainty behind a claim.

blocks.tip: Reach for the conditional when rewriting for a cautious or general audience that needs to feel the claim is measured, not overstated — but drop it for expert or legal audiences who expect flat, committed statements.

passages.title: Trois versions du même rapport
passages.french: Le service de presse d'un institut de recherche affiche, depuis peu, une règle interne un peu insolite : tout rapport scientifique destiné à publication doit être réécrit trois fois, jamais une seule. La première version, la plus dense, reste réservée aux pairs, aux comités de lecture, aux revues spécialisées ; elle assume un lecteur qui maîtrise déjà le vocabulaire, ne s'embarrasse d'aucune définition, et privilégie la concision jusqu'à l'ellipse. La deuxième version s'adresse aux décideurs et aux journalistes : le jargon y disparaît presque entièrement, remplacé par des équivalents courants, mais chaque simplification est explicitement signalée en note, pour qu'aucun lecteur pressé ne prenne un raccourci pour une nuance perdue. La troisième version, enfin, vise le grand public : les phrases raccourcissent encore, les exemples concrets se multiplient, et le ton, tout en restant rigoureux, s'autorise une pointe de conversationnel qu'aucune des deux premières versions n'aurait tolérée. Ce qui frappe, en comparant les trois textes côte à côte, ce n'est pas que l'un serait plus vrai que les autres, mais que chacun dit exactement la même chose, avec une honnêteté égale, à des lecteurs dont on a simplement pris la peine d'imaginer ce qu'ils savaient déjà. Le responsable du service résume la méthode d'une formule qu'il répète à chaque nouvelle recrue : on ne réécrit pas pour édulcorer, on réécrit pour que personne, à aucun niveau de lecture, ne soit laissé de côté.
passages.english: The press office of a research institute has recently adopted a somewhat unusual internal rule: every scientific report intended for publication must be rewritten three times, never just once. The first version, the densest, is reserved for peers, editorial boards, and specialist journals; it assumes a reader who already masters the vocabulary, bothers with no definitions, and favours conciseness to the point of ellipsis. The second version addresses decision-makers and journalists: the jargon almost entirely disappears, replaced by everyday equivalents, but every simplification is explicitly flagged in a note, so that no rushed reader mistakes a shortcut for a lost nuance. The third version, finally, targets the general public: sentences shorten further, concrete examples multiply, and the tone, while remaining rigorous, allows itself a touch of conversational ease that neither of the first two versions would have tolerated. What is striking, comparing the three texts side by side, is not that one would be truer than the others, but that each says exactly the same thing, with equal honesty, to readers whose existing knowledge someone simply took the trouble to imagine. The head of the department sums up the method in a phrase he repeats to every new recruit: we do not rewrite to water things down, we rewrite so that no one, at any level of reading, gets left behind.
